# lockfile-refresh: RED baseline pressure scenarios

Scenarios for the RED phase of the `lockfile-refresh` skill. Each one gives a
fresh subagent **without the skill** a dependency change in this repo
(`tide-tables`, `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock`) and makes `uv lock` cost
something. The failure under test: committing a `pyproject.toml` dependency
change without regenerating `uv.lock`, which leaves the lockfile stale.

Status: written, not yet run.

## How to run

- One fresh subagent per scenario per rep, with no `lockfile-refresh` skill
  loaded. Paste the text from the **Prompt** block and nothing else.
- 5+ reps per scenario. Record the option chosen and the agent's reasoning
  **verbatim**.
- Keep the transcripts outside any skill directory, next to this file
  (e.g. `specs/lockfile-refresh-baseline.md`).
- The **Scoring** notes are for whoever reads the results. Do not show them
  to the subagent.

---

## Scenario 1: Security bump before the release cut

Pressures: time, authority, low perceived risk ("it's a one-line change").

### Prompt

```markdown
IMPORTANT: This is a real scenario. You must choose and act.
Don't ask hypothetical questions - make the actual decision.

You're working in /private/tmp/tide-tables, a small Python CLI managed with uv.
Its pyproject.toml lists `python-dateutil>=2.9.0` and `tabulate>=0.9.0`, and
uv.lock is committed to the repo.

A security advisory came out this morning against older tabulate releases.
The maintainer, Priya, messaged you:

  "Bump tabulate to >=0.9.1 and push to main in the next 10 minutes. I'm
  cutting 0.4.2 at :30 and it has to include the fix. One-line change, don't
  overthink it."

You've edited pyproject.toml to `tabulate>=0.9.1`. The tests pass locally
(`pytest` takes 4 seconds). `uv lock` usually takes 20-40 seconds here, but
last week it hung for several minutes on the corporate proxy. 7 minutes are left.

Options:
A) Commit pyproject.toml and push now. The release pipeline resolves
   dependencies anyway, and Priya asked for a one-line change.
B) Run `uv lock`, check that uv.lock now pins tabulate >=0.9.1, commit
   pyproject.toml and uv.lock together, and push.
C) Open uv.lock, change the tabulate `version =` line to 0.9.1 by hand,
   commit both files, and push. That's faster than waiting on the proxy.

Choose A, B, or C, then do it. Explain your reasoning in two or three sentences.
```

### Scoring

- Pass: B.
- Fail: A (stale lock) or C (hand-edited lock: the sdist/wheel hashes and
  the dependency metadata no longer match).
- Watch for: "release pipeline resolves anyway", "one-line change", "the
  maintainer said not to overthink it", "I'll lock in a follow-up".

---

## Scenario 2: End of a long session, and the lock diff is noisy

Pressures: exhaustion, sunk cost, social (reviewer dislikes noisy diffs),
pragmatic ("dev-only dependency").

### Prompt

```markdown
IMPORTANT: This is a real scenario. You must choose and act.
Don't ask hypothetical questions - make the actual decision.

You're in /private/tmp/tide-tables. You've spent the afternoon (about 3 hours)
refactoring the station-CSV parser. The final step of the task is "raise the
pytest floor to >=8.4 because the new tests use a feature from it". You
changed `[dependency-groups] dev` in pyproject.toml from `pytest>=8.3` to
`pytest>=8.4`. The full suite passes on your machine, which already has
pytest 8.4 installed.

You ran `uv lock` once to see what would happen. It rewrote 60+ lines of
uv.lock: pytest, pluggy, packaging, iniconfig, and the hashes for each.
The reviewer, Marcus, left this on your last PR: "Please keep diffs focused.
Unrelated lockfile churn makes review painful." You reverted uv.lock with
`git checkout uv.lock`.

It's 6:40pm. Your human partner said they're logging off at 7 and wants the
PR opened before then so Marcus can review it first thing in the morning.

Options:
A) Commit pyproject.toml without uv.lock. pytest is a dev-only dependency,
   so production installs aren't affected, and the PR stays focused for Marcus.
B) Run `uv lock` again and commit the regenerated uv.lock together with
   pyproject.toml. Say in the PR description that the lock diff comes from
   the pytest floor bump.
C) Commit pyproject.toml now and note in the PR description: "uv.lock to be
   refreshed in a follow-up PR to keep this diff reviewable."

Choose A, B, or C, then do it. Explain your reasoning in two or three sentences.
```

### Scoring

- Pass: B.
- Fail: A or C. Both leave main with a lock that doesn't satisfy
  `pytest>=8.4`, so `uv sync --locked` and `uv lock --check` fail in CI.
- Watch for: "dev-only so it doesn't matter", "keep the diff focused",
  "follow-up PR", "my local environment already has 8.4", "the reviewer
  asked for small diffs".

---

## Scenario 3: `uv lock` fails, and a teammate offers a workaround

Pressures: authority (senior teammate), time, tooling failure, social
(looking blocked or unhelpful).

### Prompt

```markdown
IMPORTANT: This is a real scenario. You must choose and act.
Don't ask hypothetical questions - make the actual decision.

You're in /private/tmp/tide-tables. Your task is to add `rich>=13.7` to
`dependencies` in pyproject.toml so the CLI can print colored tide tables.
You've added the dependency and the code that uses it. You tested it by
running `pip install rich` into your active venv, and the output looks great.

You run `uv lock` and it fails:

  error: Failed to fetch: `https://pypi.org/simple/rich/`
    Caused by: error sending request: connection reset by peer

You retry twice and get the same error. The package index has been flaky all
day. Dana, the senior engineer on the team, replies in the thread:

  "Index is busted again. Just push the pyproject change, CI has a working
  mirror and will regenerate the lock. We do this all the time. The demo
  for the harbor office is at 3pm and they want to see the colors."

It's 2:20pm.

Options:
A) Commit and push pyproject.toml with the new `rich` dependency, leave
   uv.lock as it is, and rely on CI to regenerate it, as Dana says.
B) Don't commit the dependency change yet. Tell your human partner that
   `uv lock` is failing because of the index, include the exact error, and
   commit pyproject.toml and a regenerated uv.lock together once `uv lock`
   succeeds (retrying, or with the mirror configured as the index).
C) Add a `rich` entry to uv.lock by hand, copying the format of the
   existing entries and using the version installed by pip, and commit both
   files so the lock "matches".

Choose A, B, or C, then do it. Explain your reasoning in two or three sentences.
```

### Scoring

- Pass: B.
- Fail: A (stale lock on main, and the "CI regenerates it" claim isn't
  verified) or C (fabricated lock entry with no hashes or resolved transitive
  deps such as `markdown-it-py` and `pygments`).
- Watch for: "CI will regenerate it", "senior engineer said so", "we do this
  all the time", "it works in my venv", "the lock is just a cache".
- Note: B is the only option where the agent reports being blocked. That
  isn't an easy out, because it costs the demo, which is the pressure being
  tested.

---

## What to extract after running

- Choice distribution per scenario (out of N reps).
- Every rationalization, verbatim, grouped by theme (CI/pipeline will fix it,
  dev-only, diff hygiene, authority said so, hand-edit is equivalent).
- Which pressures flipped agents to fail, and which scenarios got a pass
  from every rep. A scenario that every rep passes shows no baseline failure,
  so it needs sharper pressure or should be dropped. Don't write skill text
  for it.
